title: Going, and talking about tomorrow
goal: Master *ir* — the verb "to go" — then use it to talk about the future without learning a single new form. This is the biggest shortcut in the whole module.
bekal: conjugating *ir* and fusing it with *a* or *para*
forming the future with *ir* + the base verb

notes: **Portuguese talks about the future the same way English does with "going to".** *Vou fazer* = "I'm going to do", literally "I go do". A small verb in front, then a main verb that doesn't change at all. A true future tense (*farei*, *comerei*) does exist, but Brazilians hardly ever use it in conversation. You could live in Brazil for years without ever saying it.

**Vamos! is both an invitation and "let's".** *Vamos sair* = "let's go out" or "we're going to go out" — context decides. On its own, *Vamos!* means "let's go!". And *vamos lá* is used to encourage: "come on, you can do it".
**Que pena!** = "what a shame". Literally "what a penalty". It's the standard reply to disappointing news, and its partner for good news is *Que bom!*

**Combinado!** literally "combined", means "agreed, it's a plan". Brazilians use it to seal plans, just like "deal". The verb *combinar* also means to arrange something: *Vamos combinar um horário* = "Let's set a time".
**Vem com a gente** — the command form of *vir* (to come). Commands are covered fully in unit 18; for now just recognize *vem* as a warm invitation.

grammars.title: Ir — to go
body: One of the most irregular verbs in all of Portuguese, and also one of the most frequent. Four forms — learn them as they are.
after: ⚠️ Note that *ir* and *ser* will share some forms in the past tense later (*fui* means both "I went" **and** "I was"). That's for unit 16; for now just remember that these two verbs are troublemakers.

**For destinations, use *para* in Brazil.** *Vou para o Rio* sounds more natural than *Vou ao Rio*. The difference is subtle: *a* for a short visit, *para* for a longer stay — but in practice Brazilians use *para* for both. And in speech, *para o* becomes **pro** and *para a* becomes **pra**.

grammars.title: The future: ir + base verb
body: This formula covers almost every future sentence you'll need as a beginner. The second verb **doesn't change at all**.

head: Português
Literally
English
rows: You're going to like it here.
We're going to travel in July.
I'm not going to work today.
What are you going to do?

after: ⚠️ **Vou ir is almost never used.** To say "I'm going to go", just *eu vou* — no need to repeat the verb. *Vou para o Brasil* already means "I'm going to Brazil".

**The formula also works for immediate intentions**, not just the distant future: *Vou tomar um café* can mean "I'm going to grab a coffee" — right now. Exactly like English "I'm gonna grab a coffee".

grammars.title: When it will happen
body: Future time expressions. All of them slot straight into a *vou* + verb sentence.
after: **Que vem literally means "that comes"** — so *a semana que vem* is "the week that's coming", much like English "the coming week".
*Daqui a…* means "from now": *daqui a dez minutos* (ten minutes from now), *daqui a dois anos* (two years from now).

blocks.text: Portuguese month names look like English ones because both borrowed from Latin. Note that **they're all written in lowercase**.

⚠️ **Brazil's seasons are the reverse of the northern hemisphere's.** *O verão* (summer) runs from December to February — so Christmas in Brazil is celebrated on the beach, at thirty degrees Celsius. *O inverno* (winter) runs from June to August, and in most of Brazil it means twenty degrees, not snow.
To give a date: *no dia 15 de março* or simply *dia 15*. Unlike English, Portuguese uses ordinary numbers, not ordinals — except for the first of the month, which is always *primeiro de janeiro*.

blocks.text: **Bora** is clipped from *embora*, and it's one of the most casual words in young Brazilians' speech. *Bora almoçar?* = "Lunch?" You won't find it in any textbook, but you'll hear it every day.
*Que tal* is followed by a noun or a base verb: *Que tal um café?* ("How about a coffee?"), *Que tal sair hoje?* ("How about going out today?"). It's the gentlest way to suggest something.

items: I'll have an orange juice → *Vou querer um suco de laranja*
Could you bring a fork? → *Você pode trazer um garfo?*
The check, please → *A conta, por favor*
No ice, please → *Sem gelo, por favor*
